results.title: The two clocks behind every GPU rental quote – TensorCurve
results.author: Justin
highlights:
A price record should include three ... The observation time tells you when the offer was seen. The start date tells you when access begins. The duration tells you the contracted period of access or payment.

...

## Read a published commitment curve

A term curve changes contract duration while holding the product constant. A forward-start curve instead changes when access begins. The homepage uses Verda’s H100 SXM5 80GB instance with 30 CPUs and 120GB RAM. Its published on-demand base is $3.25 per hour for one GPU.

The supplier lists discounts of 2%, 3%, 4% and 8% for commitments of one, three, six and twelve months. Applying those discounts gives $3.1850, $3.1525, $3.1200 and $2.9900 per GPU-hour. TensorCurve calculates these values; the source publishes the base and discount schedule. The chart uses equal spacing for duration categories, not a continuous calendar axis.

Source checked 13 September 2026: Verda official pricing. Calculations use the published on-demand rate and reserved discounts; they are not separately quoted transaction prices.

This is one supplier’s tariff-derived commitment curve. It does not measure the global GPU market. The pricing table does not establish a region-specific offer or a guaranteed start date. Those fields remain unverified. A price for a twelve-month commitment does not tell us what a twelve-month contract beginning next December would cost.

...

Payment commitment and capacity reservation also need separate fields. A lower effective rate does not, by itself, establish that a particular machine will be ready for a particular workload on a particular day.

results.title: The same GPU, at very different prices · infratoapp
highlights:
## The finding

30 GPU models are rented on-demand by 3 or more of the providers listed here. On every one of them, the providers disagree about the price — and on most, they disagree by more than a rounding error.

The median gap between the cheapest and dearest seller of an identical card is 3.8×. The widest is the V100-16GB: $0.24 per GPU-hour at Verda (DataCrunch) against $2.85 at Runcrate, a gap of 11.8×. An H100 SXM 80GB — the card most of this market is actually built on — runs from $2.16 to $6.16 across 13 sellers, a gap of 2.8×.

These are headline on-demand rates, before any commitment discount, for the same part. Not a similar part, not a different memory configuration, and not one region against another.

...

Four constraints decide whether a number like this means anything, and each one removes rows we would rather have kept.

On-demand only. A spot rate is a different product and a committed rate is a different contract; putting them in one range would compare things nobody chooses between.

One rate per seller per card, their cheapest. A provider listing an H100 at four instance sizes is one seller with one headline rate. Counting each instance size separately would let a single price list manufacture a spread on its own.

Headline rates rather than regional ones. Comparing Virginia against Frankfurt and calling the difference a market would be a mistake about geography wearing the costume of a finding.

A minimum of 3 sellers. A couple of providers disagreeing is an anecdote. This bar is what reduces the set to the 30 cards compared, and it is the constraint we would relax last.

...

Across the 30 cards compared, the lowest rate tends to sit with marketplaces and community clouds rather than managed providers. The widest gap, on the V100-16GB, is Verda (DataCrunch) against Runcrate.

That is a fact about price and nothing else. It says nothing about availability when you need a whole cluster at once, about what happens when an instance is reclaimed, about support, or about whether the network between your nodes is any good. Those differences are most of why the dearer providers exist, and none of them are visible in a per-hour rate.

So this is not a buying recommendation, and there is no "best value" column anywhere on this site. The number tells you what to ask about, not what to choose.

results.title: DataCrunch Alternative (2026): GPU Prices vs LowCostGPU
highlights:
# DataCrunch alternative: same NVIDIA GPUs, fixed prices 30% under the market

DataCrunch renamed itself Verda in November 2025; datacrunch.io now redirects to verda.com, and the team, infrastructure and customer accounts carried over unchanged. Founded in Helsinki in 2018, Verda owns and operates its own datacenters rather than reselling capacity, with two sites in Helsinki and one in Reykjanesbaer, Iceland, on renewable power. It raised $117M in 2026 to build what it calls a European hyperscaler and expand into the UK, the US and Asia; a fourth Nordic site (Akaa, Finland) is announced but not yet live.

results.title: European GPU Clouds: 8 Alternatives to AWS and Azure ...
results.author: Mélanie Dallé
highlights:
- The eight European GPU cloud alternatives to shortlist against AWS and Azure: Scaleway and OVHcloud (EU-owned full-service clouds with managed Kubernetes, H100 and L40S), Nscale and Verda (AI-first clouds with H100/H200/GB200-class fleets), Hetzner and IONOS (cheaper EU-owned capacity with a narrower GPU catalogue), Exoscale (compliance-focused, EU-owned), and the Vast.ai/RunPod marketplace tier for burst and experimentation.
- On published on-demand list prices in EU regions, European GPU specialists undercut AWS p5 and Azure ND H100 v5 per GPU-hour, and marketplace hosts go lower still. Hyperscaler list prices are pre-discount, so compare against your actual Savings Plan or committed-use rate, not the sticker.
- An EU region on AWS or Azure delivers data residency, not corporate or jurisdictional independence: the operating entity's ultimate parent stays US-headquartered, which is the gap AWS European Sovereign Cloud and Microsoft's EU Data Boundary were built to close.
- Capacity, not price, is usually the binding constraint. Most European H100/H200 fleets are allocated by quota request, hourly reservation, or multi-month committed cluster, so confirm region-level availability in writing before you benchmark cost.
- Egress and data gravity, not compute, decide whether a migration pays back. Price per-GB transfer out of your current provider against a multi-terabyte training set before you compare GPU-hours, and check what the EU Data Act's switching rules change for your exit.
- Qovery does not sell GPUs. Qovery is the developer platform layer running inside your own cloud account (BYOC) on AWS, GCP, Azure, Scaleway, or any existing Kubernetes cluster, so you can move GPU workloads to whichever EU provider has capacity at the right price while keeping one deployment workflow.

...

- Scaleway (France, Iliad group): H100 PCIe, H100 SXM, L40S and L4 behind managed Kubernetes (Kapsule) with public per-hour pricing. Best for EU teams that want a full cloud and GPUs in one console.
- OVHcloud (France): H100, A100, L40S single cards plus 8xH200 nodes, managed Kubernetes (MKS), free egress and public pricing. Best for the widest published EU GPU catalogue.
- Nscale: an AI-first cloud running hydro-powered data centres in Glomfjord, Norway (EEA), with H100, H200 and GB200/GB300-class systems sold by quote. Best for large committed training clusters.
- Verda (formerly DataCrunch, Finland): public on-demand and spot pricing for H100, H200, B200 and GB300. Best for price-sensitive training and fine-tuning with transparent rates.
- Hetzner (Germany): monthly dedicated GPU servers (NVIDIA RTX 4000 SFF Ada, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell), not hourly cloud. Best for cheap, steady inference you can commit to monthly.
- IONOS (Germany, United Internet): NVIDIA H200 cloud VMs at a flat per-GPU-hour rate, EU hosting and ISO 27001. Best for regulated EU workloads that want a simple H200 rate.
- Exoscale (Austria, A1 Group): GPU families around NVIDIA A40, A30, V100 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell across Frankfurt, Vienna, Geneva and Zagreb. Best for compliance-heavy EU workloads that do not need H100 or H200.
- Vast.ai and RunPod (GPU marketplaces): H100 SXM and A100 by the hour at the cheapest headline rates, where European hosting, DPA coverage and uptime depend on the individual host you rent from. Best for burst and experimentation, not regulated production.

...

On published EU on-demand list prices checked in September 2026, AWS charges roughly $7.36 per H100 GPU-hour (p5.48xlarge at $58.89/hour for 8 GPUs in eu-north-1, Stockholm) and Azure roughly $15.98 per H100 GPU-hour (ND96isr H100 v5 at $127.82/hour for 8 GPUs in West Europe). European specialists list H100 far below both, with Scaleway around EUR 2.87, OVHcloud at $2.99 and Verda at $3.25 per GPU-hour, and the Vast.ai/RunPod marketplace tier dips lower still at the cost of predictable quality. Read marketplace rates as a floor, not a guarantee.

...

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Verda H100 SXM5 | Finland | 1 | $3.25 (spot $1.63) | H200 $4.00, B200 $6.11, A100 80GB $1.79 (Verda pricing) |

| Hetzner GEX131 (RTX PRO 6000) | Germany / Finland | 1 | ~EUR 1.22 at 24/7 (~EUR 890/mo ÷ 730h) | Monthly dedicated, not hourly; GEX44 (RTX 4000 Ada) ~EUR 184/mo (Hetzner GPU servers) |

...

A cheap European per-GPU-hour can hide what it leaves out, too. Check whether the rate includes fast block storage IOPS, the interconnect you actually need (PCIe H100 and SXM H100 are not interchangeable for multi-GPU work, and InfiniBand or RDMA fabric is often a separate line), your support tier, and the idle hours between jobs. Spot and interruptible capacity, like Verda's H100 spot at $1.63 against $3.25 on-demand, is a genuine discount only when you checkpoint. A preempted multi-day run with no checkpoints can throw away days of progress, which costs far more than the hours you saved.

results.title: Nvidia's move into financial backing of AI infrastructure reshapes industry risk landscape | Noah Intelligence
results.author: Jaimie Isaias Technology Editor
highlights:
Huang’s blog post offered the clearest explanation of what Nvidia says it is trying to build. Writing on the company site, (blogs.nvidia.com) he argued that AI compute should be treated as a long-lived infrastructure asset with resale and rental value, not simply as hardware sold once and forgotten. To make that case, Nvidia pointed to strengthening rental economics: one-year H100 pricing had risen from about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to about $2.35 in March 2026, while median on-demand pricing had climbed from roughly $2.00 to $2.70 by June; reported B200 cloud rates, the company said, were higher still. Huang also tried to head off criticism that the arrangement amounted to circular finance, saying the capital providers would independently assess demand, utilisation, cash flow and residual value, and that any Nvidia support would be limited and project-specific.

...

The Ohio deal was not the only sign that Nvidia was moving down the financing chain. Data Center Dynamics, (datacenterdynamics.com) citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that Nvidia had paused some revenue-sharing arrangements with AI cloud providers that were unveiled in July. Under those deals, DCD said, Nvidia acted as a financial backstop for operators building large compute clusters, took a share of the revenue, and in some cases agreed to rent back unused GPUs at a fixed rate. Firmus and Sharon AI were identified as early adopters, with Firmus deploying 170,000 GPUs in Batam, Indonesia, and Sharon AI deploying 40,000 GB300 GPUs. Nvidia told DCD: "The new business model we introduced in July that opens up compute access to the fast-growing AI ecosystem is still in place and continues to evolve due to high demand."

results.title: Nebius hikes AI cloud prices again as demand for computing power soars | My 95.7
results.author: Thomson Reuters
highlights:
Sept 17 (Reuters) – Cloud provider Nebius said on Thursday it will raise pay-as-you-go prices for leasing selected ​Nvidia chips from October 1, ‌marking the company’s second price hike in three months.

Demand for computing capacity to train and run AI models is surging; rival CoreWeave ‌said ​earlier in the ⁠day that it is ⁠signing contracts at higher prices.

Here are some details:

• Rates for selected Nvidia graphics processing units will rise between ​17% and 21%.

• On-demand rates for some central processing units, made ⁠by AMD and Intel, ⁠and memory offerings have also ​been hiked.

• Prices of some CPU-only instances ​will rise by 25% and those ‌of memory offerings by about 41%, the company said.

• The Amsterdam-based neocloud firm said that customers reserving large-scale clusters ⁠for multiple months can receive commitment discounts.

• Nebius’ price increases follow a quarter of rapid ⁠growth ‌in its AI cloud business, ⁠as the company signed four ​customer ‌contracts averaging more than $1 billion ​each.

• Neocloud ⁠firms like Nebius rent out high-powered chips and data center infrastructure needed for AI models.
